han.name: Han court
han.note: Deliberately the palest thing on the map -- near-neutral, so the warlords read as colour against it. The imperial government as an independent actor: whoever holds the Emperor. Shrinks to nothing after Cao Cao takes him to Xuchang in ch. 14.

shu.name: Shu Han
shu.note: Liu Bei's following, from two men in a Zhuo county garden to the western empire.

wei.name: Cao Wei
wei.note: Cao Cao's power, later the Wei dynasty.

wu.name: Eastern Wu
wu.note: The Sun family's south-east, from Sun Jian through Sun Ce to Sun Quan.

yellowturban.name: Yellow Turbans
yellowturban.note: Zhang Jue's rising. Territory here means districts in revolt, not administration.

lijueguosi.name: Li Jue and Guo Si
lijueguosi.note: Dong Zhuo's officers, who inherit Chang'an and the Emperor after ch. 9.

taoqian.name: Tao Qian
taoqian.note: Xuzhou, willed to Liu Bei in ch. 12.

liubiao.name: Liu Biao
liubiao.note: Jing province, the buffer Liu Bei shelters in for seven years.

liuzhang.name: Liu Zhang
liuzhang.note: Yi province, inherited from his father Liu Yan. Absorbed by Liu Bei in ch. 65.

xiliang.name: Ma Teng and Han Sui
xiliang.note: The Liang province horsemen of the north-west.

zhanglu.name: Zhang Lu
zhanglu.note: The Five Pecks of Rice theocracy in Hanzhong.

nanman.name: Nanman
nanman.note: Meng Huo's southern tribes, campaigned against in ch. 87-90.

unaligned.name: Unaligned
unaligned.note: Fallback for figures with no standing allegiance.

liubei.note: A mat-weaver claiming descent from Prince Jing of Zhongshan. The novel's moral centre and its most restless traveller.

guanyu.note: Later deified as the god of war.

zhaoyun.note: First met in ch. 7 fighting for Gongsun Zan; does not join Liu Bei for good until ch. 28.

zhugeliang.note: 諸葛 is read Gia Cát in Vietnamese, not the regular Chư Cát.

liushan.role: Second and last emperor of Shu

caocao.role: Chancellor of Han; founder of Wei
caocao.note: Judged in the novel as 'a capable minister in a peaceful age, a treacherous hero in a chaotic one'.

xiahoudun.note: Swallows his own eye at Xiapi, ch. 18.

dianwei.note: Dies covering Cao Cao's escape at Wan, ch. 16.

zhangliao.note: Lü Bu's officer until ch. 19, then Cao Cao's best field commander.

simayi.role: Wei commander; grandfather of the Jin dynasty

jiaxu.note: Serves Dong Zhuo's officers, then Zhang Xiu, then Cao Cao, and outlives them all.

sunjian.note: Finds the Imperial Seal in a well at Luoyang, ch. 6; killed attacking Liu Biao, ch. 7.

sunce.note: Conquers the south-east in ch. 15 with borrowed troops.

taishici.note: Breaks the siege of Beihai for Kong Rong in ch. 11 before ever meeting the Sun family.

huanggai.note: Takes the beating that sells the false defection at Red Cliffs, ch. 46.

ganning.note: A river pirate before he was an admiral.

lvmeng.note: Takes Jing province from Guan Yu, ch. 75.

luxun.note: Burns Liu Bei's camps at Xiaoting, ch. 84.

emperorxian.note: Enthroned by Dong Zhuo at nine years old; a hostage of one warlord or another for the rest of his life.

wangyun.note: Author of the chain stratagem that destroys Dong Zhuo.

dongcheng.note: Receives the girdle edict in ch. 20.

hejin.note: Summons Dong Zhuo to the capital and is murdered by the eunuchs before he arrives, ch. 3.

zhangjue.note: Styles himself General of Heaven. Dies of illness mid-rebellion, ch. 2.

huaxiong.note: Killed by Guan Yu before the wine cooled, ch. 5.

yuanshao.note: Head of a family with 'three dukes in four generations', and the coalition's chosen leader.

yuanshu.note: Declares himself emperor on the strength of the stolen seal, ch. 17.

lvbu.role: The finest warrior of the age
lvbu.note: 'Among men, Lü Bu; among horses, Red Hare.' Kills two adoptive fathers.

diaochan.note: Fictional. The novel's chain stratagem turns on her; the histories know only an unnamed maid of Dong Zhuo's.

chengong.note: Releases Cao Cao, rides with him, then leaves him over the murder of Lü Boshe's family, ch. 4.

gongsunzan.note: Liu Bei's schoolfellow under Lu Zhi, and his first patron.

lvboshe.note: Killed with his whole household in ch. 4, on a misheard sentence about a pig.

luoyang.note: Han capital until Dong Zhuo burns it in ch. 6.

changan.note: Former Western Han capital; Dong Zhuo's refuge from ch. 6.

xuchang.note: Cao Cao's seat, and the Emperor's cage, from ch. 14.

ye.note: Yuan Shao's capital, later Cao Cao's northern seat.

chengdu.note: Capital of Yi province, then of Shu Han.

jianye.note: Sun Quan's capital; called Moling 秣陵 before 212.

zhuo.note: Liu Bei's home county. The peach garden oath, ch. 1.

yijing.note: Gongsun Zan's fortress, where he burns himself in ch. 21.

xiangping.note: Seat of the Gongsun family of Liaodong.

pingyuan.note: Liu Bei's first real post, granted by Gongsun Zan.

nanpi.note: Bohai commandery, Yuan Shao's original base.

puyang.note: Lü Bu's base while he holds Yan province, ch. 11-12.

beihai.note: Kong Rong's command; besieged in ch. 11.

xiaopei.note: The small town Liu Bei is repeatedly parked in.

wan.note: Nanyang. Zhang Xiu's seat; Dian Wei dies covering Cao Cao's retreat here in ch. 16.

shouchun.note: Yuan Shu's capital, and where he declares himself emperor in ch. 17.

hefei.note: The hinge of the Wei-Wu frontier for forty years.

danyang.note: The commandery that supplies the Sun family's best infantry.

chaisang.note: Sun Quan's forward headquarters during the Red Cliffs campaign.

xiangyang.note: Liu Biao's capital in Jing province.

fancheng.note: Across the Han from Xiangyang. Guan Yu's last campaign, ch. 73-76.

xinye.note: The border town Liu Biao lends Liu Bei as a shield against Cao Cao.

maicheng.note: Guan Yu is taken here, ch. 77.

hulao.note: Where the three brothers fight Lü Bu, ch. 5.

sishui.note: Hua Xiong's gate. Historically the same place as Hulao; the novel makes them two.

tongguan.note: Cao Cao against Ma Chao, ch. 58-59.

jieqiao.note: Yuan Shao against Gongsun Zan, ch. 7.

wuchao.note: Yuan Shao's granaries, burnt in ch. 30.

baima.note: Guan Yu kills Yan Liang, ch. 25.

hanzhong.note: Zhang Lu's theocracy, then the gate between Wei and Shu.

dingjun.note: Huang Zhong kills Xiahou Yuan, ch. 71.

jiange.note: The pass Jiang Wei holds while Deng Ai goes around it, ch. 117.

shangyong.note: Liu Feng and Meng Da fail to relieve Guan Yu from here, ch. 76.

jicheng.note: Seat of Liang province, the Ma family's country.

chencang.note: The fort that stops Zhuge Liang's second northern expedition, ch. 97.

qishan.note: The road Zhuge Liang takes north again and again.

jieting.note: Ma Su loses it; Zhuge Liang weeps and executes him, ch. 96.

henei.note: Henei, north of the Yellow River opposite Luoyang. Wang Kuang's coalition contingent musters here.

suanzao.note: The allied camp at Suanzao where the coalition against Dong Zhuo swears its oath, ch. 5.

chapters.title: Three Heroes Swear Brotherhood in the Peach Garden; One Victory Shatters the Rebels at Julu
summary: The empire, long divided, must unite. Under the boy emperor Ling the eunuchs rule and the harvests fail, and a Daoist healer named Zhang Jue turns a following of five hundred thousand into an army wearing yellow headscarves.

In Zhuo county a call goes out for volunteers. Three men meet before the notice board: a mat-weaver who claims imperial descent, a fugitive who killed a bully in his home county, and a butcher and wine-seller with a voice like thunder. In a peach garden behind the butcher's house they swear to die on the same day.
They raise five hundred men, ride south, and break a Yellow Turban force outside Zhuo. The rebellion is far larger than they are.
chapters.history: Zhang Jue's rising is historical, and so is its scale. The oath in the peach garden is not — the histories say only that Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei 'slept on the same mat and were as brothers'.

pins.note: Reading the call for volunteers outside the county gate.
A fugitive from Hedong, five years on the run.
Owns the peach garden, and the wine.
General of Heaven, at the head of the rising.
Marching against Zhang Jue in the north.
A colonel of the palace guard, thirty years old.
Still a frontier general in the west.

chapters.title: Zhang Fei Whips the Government Inspector; He Jin Plots to Kill the Eunuchs
summary: The rebellion is broken and the brothers are given a county post so small it is an insult. When a government inspector arrives demanding a bribe, Zhang Fei ties him to a post and flogs him with a willow switch, and the three of them are fugitives again.

At court the Emperor Ling dies. The General-in-Chief He Jin, a butcher's son raised by his sister's place in the harem, resolves to destroy the ten eunuchs who run the palace — and is talked into summoning the frontier armies to help him do it.
chapters.history: The flogging is the novel's invention, and a characteristic one: the histories give the deed to Liu Bei, who is a good deal less genial than the story lets him be.

pins.note: A county magistrate, briefly.
Flogs the inspector and takes to the road.
Summoning the frontier generals to the capital.
Urging He Jin on.
Alone in warning that this will end badly.
Receives the summons east.
Dies of illness; his brothers are hunted down.

chapters.title: Dong Zhuo Rebukes the Emperor at Wenming Garden; Li Su Tempts Lü Bu with Red Hare
summary: The eunuchs strike first: He Jin is cut down inside the palace gate. Yuan Shao and Cao Cao storm in and kill every beardless man they find, two thousand of them, and in the confusion the boy emperor is carried out of the burning capital into the dark.
It is Dong Zhuo who finds him on the road, and Dong Zhuo who brings him back — with an army from Liang province and no intention of leaving. Within days he is talking openly of setting the boy aside.
Ding Yuan opposes him, protected by his formidable adopted son. Dong Zhuo sends a horse worth a thousand pieces of gold, and Lü Bu brings him Ding Yuan's head.
chapters.history: Dong Zhuo's march on Luoyang and the massacre of the eunuchs are historical. Red Hare is real too; the story that Lü Bu was bought with it is the novel's.

pins.note: Arrives with the Liang province army and does not leave.
Kills his adoptive father Ding Yuan for a horse.
Murdered inside the palace gate.
Storms the palace; then quarrels with Dong Zhuo and rides for Bohai.
Nine years old, and about to be made emperor.

chapters.title: Deposing the Emperor, Dong Zhuo Installs Another; Cao Cao Presents a Sword and Flees
summary: Dong Zhuo deposes the young emperor, enthrones his nine-year-old brother as Emperor Xian, and has the mother and son poisoned. In council he answers objections by having the objector dragged out and killed.

Cao Cao takes a jewelled sword from Wang Yun and goes to Dong Zhuo's chamber to use it. Caught in the mirror's reflection, he kneels and presents the blade as a gift instead, then rides east before the story can be tested.

On the road he is sheltered by his father's sworn brother Lü Boshe, hears knives being sharpened, and kills the household — nine people — before he sees the pig tied up for the feast. He kills Lü Boshe too, on the road, to keep him from talking.
chapters.history: The sword and the mirror are the novel's. Cao Cao's flight is historical; so is a version of the killing at Lü Boshe's house, which even the sympathetic sources record.

pins.note: Fails to kill Dong Zhuo; rides east to raise an army.
Releases Cao Cao, rides with him, and leaves him after Lü Boshe.
Killed on the road with his whole household.
Enthroned at nine.
Lends the sword, and begins to wait.

chapters.title: Cao Cao Rallies the Lords; Three Heroes Fight Lü Bu at Hulao Pass
summary: Cao Cao's forged summons brings eighteen lords and their armies to the camp at Suanzao. They elect Yuan Shao their chief, swear an oath, and immediately begin to quarrel about supplies.

At Sishui Pass Dong Zhuo's champion Hua Xiong kills every man sent against him. A nameless bowman in Gongsun Zan's train asks to try; Cao Cao pours him wine to send him off; he returns with the head and the wine is still warm.
At Hulao Pass Lü Bu breaks every commander in turn until all three brothers ride at him at once, and even then he only withdraws.
chapters.history: The coalition existed and achieved almost nothing. Guan Yu never met Hua Xiong, who was killed by Sun Jian's troops, and the three-on-one at Hulao is pure novel — the most famous fight in the book has no history behind it at all.

pins.note: Elected commander of the alliance.
Forged the summons that raised it.
Leads the vanguard against Sishui Pass.
Arrives in Gongsun Zan's train, unranked.
Kills Hua Xiong before the wine cools.
Holds the pass until Guan Yu.
Fights all three brothers at once.
In charge of supply, and withholds it from Sun Jian.

chapters.title: Burning the Capital, Dong Zhuo Commits an Atrocity; Hiding the Seal, Sun Jian Breaks Faith
summary: Rather than hold Luoyang, Dong Zhuo burns it. Several million people are driven west along the road to Chang'an with cavalry at their backs; the imperial tombs are dug up for their grave goods; the city burns for days.
Sun Jian, first into the ruins, finds a woman's body in a palace well with a box at her neck, and in the box the Imperial Hereditary Seal. He swears an oath that he has nothing, and starts for home.
Yuan Shao, who has been told, tries to take it from him. The alliance breaks up without ever reaching Chang'an.
chapters.history: The burning of Luoyang and the forced migration are historical, and the histories are no gentler about them than the novel is. Sun Jian's discovery of the seal is recorded in one source and doubted by others.

pins.note: Burns the capital behind him.
Carried west with the court.
Finds the Imperial Seal in a well.
Pursues alone and is ambushed; the other lords will not follow.

chapters.title: Yuan Shao Fights Gongsun Zan at the Pan River; Sun Jian Crosses the Yangtze to Attack Liu Biao
summary: The alliance turns on itself. Yuan Shao takes Ji province by a trick and then meets Gongsun Zan at the bridge over the Pan River, where Gongsun Zan is unhorsed and about to die — and is saved by a young officer in white, a stranger, who gives his name as Zhao Yun of Changshan.
In the south, Yuan Shu goads Sun Jian into attacking Liu Biao. Sun Jian pursues too far into the hills at Xianshan and is crushed under a rockfall and a volley of arrows. He is thirty-seven.
chapters.history: Both battles are historical. Zhao Yun's arrival at the bridge is the novel's staging — a way of putting him on the board early, and in Liu Bei's line of sight.

pins.note: Takes Ji province, then fights Gongsun Zan at the bridge.
Unhorsed, and saved by a stranger.
First appearance: a young officer in white.
Killed in the hills south of Xiangyang, aged thirty-seven.
Seventeen, and now head of the family.

chapters.title: Wang Yun Lays the Chain Stratagem; Dong Zhuo Storms out of the Phoenix Pavilion
summary: Wang Yun, weeping alone in his garden at the state of the empire, finds his singing-girl Diaochan weeping too, and asks her to do a thing no army has managed.

He promises her to Lü Bu and then presents her to Dong Zhuo, and lets each of them find out. She plays them against each other with complete composure — a look here, a tear there — until Lü Bu, hidden in the Phoenix Pavilion, sees what he takes for proof, and Dong Zhuo hurls a halberd at his head.
chapters.history: Diaochan is fictional. The histories record only that Lü Bu had an affair with one of Dong Zhuo's maids and lived in fear of being found out — which was enough for Wang Yun to work with.

pins.note: Sets the chain stratagem in motion.
Promised to Lü Bu, given to Dong Zhuo.
Between the capital and his treasure fortress.

chapters.title: Lü Bu Kills the Tyrant; Li Jue and Guo Si Sack the Capital
summary: Lü Bu kills Dong Zhuo in the palace gateway, in front of the court, with the abdication decree still in his hand. The body is exposed in the market; a lamp is set in its navel and burns for days on its own fat.

Then Wang Yun refuses amnesty to Dong Zhuo's officers, and Jia Xu tells them the only remaining option: 'Go back and take Chang'an. If it fails you can run then.' It does not fail. Wang Yun is killed, Lü Bu is driven out to wander, and Li Jue and Guo Si divide the Emperor between them.
chapters.history: Almost all of this is historical, including the lamp. Jia Xu's advice is recorded, and later Chinese historians blamed him personally for another decade of war.

pins.note: Killed in the palace gateway.
Driven out; begins seven years of wandering.
Refuses the amnesty, and is killed for it.
Gives the advice that costs the empire another decade.
Changes captors again.

chapters.title: Ma Teng Raises Troops for the Throne; Cao Cao Marches to Avenge His Father
summary: Ma Teng and Han Sui come east out of Liang province in the Emperor's name and are beaten back. Cao Cao, meanwhile, takes Yan province, absorbs three hundred thousand surrendered Yellow Turbans into an army, and begins to look like a power.

He sends for his father. Tao Qian of Xuzhou provides an escort, the escort murders the old man for his baggage, and Cao Cao comes east swearing to put the whole province to the sword. He very nearly does.
chapters.history: The massacres in Xuzhou are historical and were enormous; the novel does not soften them. Sources disagree on whether Tao Qian ordered the killing or merely failed to prevent it.

pins.note: Takes Yan province and an army of surrendered rebels.
Joins Cao Cao.
Marches east for the Emperor and is beaten back.
His escort murders Cao Cao's father.

chapters.title: Liu Bei Rescues Kong Rong at Beihai; Lü Bu Defeats Cao Cao at Puyang
summary: Kong Rong, besieged in Beihai by rebels, is broken out by a single rider — Taishi Ci, repaying a kindness done to his mother — and then sends to Liu Bei for help. Liu Bei's reaction to being asked is the most revealing line he has: 'Does Kong Rong know there is a Liu Bei in the world?'
He goes on to Xuzhou to lift Cao Cao's siege, and finds it lifted for him: Lü Bu, prompted by Chen Gong, has taken Yan province while Cao Cao's back was turned, and Cao Cao must go home.
chapters.history: Historical in outline. The novel gives Liu Bei the rescue of both Beihai and Xuzhou; the record is thinner and less flattering to everyone.

pins.note: Rides to Beihai, then to Xuzhou.
Still Gongsun Zan's officer.
Besieged, and rescued.
Breaks the siege line alone.
Abandons the Xuzhou campaign to save his own province.
Seizes Yan province behind Cao Cao.
The mind behind the seizure.

chapters.title: Tao Qian Yields Xuzhou Three Times; Cao Cao Fights Lü Bu at a Great Battle
summary: Tao Qian, dying, tries three times to hand Xuzhou to Liu Bei, who three times refuses it, and accepts only when there is no one left to refuse to. It is the first territory he has ever held.

Cao Cao and Lü Bu tear Yan province apart between them. Cao Cao is nearly killed at Puyang, burned and unhorsed, and saved by Dian Wei; a locust year starves both armies into breaking off; and Lü Bu, beaten, goes to Xuzhou to ask shelter of Liu Bei — who gives it.
chapters.history: The three refusals are the novel elaborating a real handover into a set-piece about Liu Bei's character. The locust famine of 194 is historical and was as decisive as any battle.

pins.note: Accepts Xuzhou at the third asking.
Dies, having given the province away.
Nearly burned to death in the gate.
Carries him out.
Beaten by famine as much as by Cao Cao.

chapters.title: Li Jue and Guo Si Fight; the Emperor Flees East
summary: The two men who hold the capital between them fall out over a jar of wine and a jealous wife, and fight in the streets of Chang'an for months. One holds the Emperor; the other kidnaps the entire court to even the score.

The Emperor escapes east with a starving procession of officials, is caught at the Yellow River crossing, and reaches the ruins of Luoyang with almost nobody left. The court sets up in the burnt shell of the old capital and the ministers gather firewood themselves.
chapters.history: Historical, and the novel understates it if anything. The flight from Chang'an in 195-196 is one of the grimmest episodes of the period.

pins.note: Reaches the ruins of his capital with nothing.
One of the few who gets the Emperor out.
Watching the road from Luoyang.

chapters.title: Cao Cao Moves the Court to Xuchang; Lü Bu Takes Xuzhou by Night
summary: Cao Cao arrives at Luoyang, feeds the court, and proposes a move to Xuchang where the granaries are. The Emperor agrees, because there is nothing else to agree to. From this point Cao Cao issues orders in the Emperor's name and his rivals must either obey them or be rebels.

One such order sends Liu Bei against Yuan Shu. He goes, leaving Zhang Fei to hold Xuzhou; Zhang Fei gets drunk, whips his officer Cao Bao, and Cao Bao opens the gate to Lü Bu. Liu Bei comes back to nothing, and takes shelter in Xiaopei — from his own guest.
chapters.history: The move to Xuchang is the pivot of the whole period: whoever held the Emperor could make his wars legal. Lü Bu's seizure of Xuzhou is historical; the drunken flogging is the novel's explanation for it.

pins.note: Takes the Emperor to Xuchang, and the initiative with him.
Argued for the move.
Loses Xuzhou while away campaigning.
Lost the city drunk.
Takes Xuzhou from the man who sheltered him.

chapters.title: Taishi Ci Fights the Little Conqueror; Sun Ce Cuts Out a Kingdom
summary: Sun Ce pawns his father's Imperial Seal to Yuan Shu for three thousand men and crosses the Yangtze with them. In a year he has the whole south-east.

At Shenting he and Taishi Ci fight alone in the hills until Sun Ce has Taishi Ci's halberd and Taishi Ci has Sun Ce's helmet, and neither can throw the other; Sun Ce takes him prisoner later and makes him a friend the same day. He lets him go on his word to return, and everyone tells him he is a fool, and Taishi Ci comes back at noon exactly.
chapters.history: Substantially historical, including the release of Taishi Ci on parole. The seal was really used as security for the loan.

pins.note: Crosses the Yangtze with three thousand borrowed men.
Joins him with troops and grain; they are the same age.
Fights Sun Ce to a standstill, then serves him.
Fourteen.
Holds the Imperial Seal as security, and begins to have ideas.

chapters.title: Lü Bu Shoots the Halberd at the Gate; Cao Cao Is Defeated at the River Yu
summary: Yuan Shu sends an army against Liu Bei at Xiaopei. Lü Bu, who wants neither of them strong, plants his halberd a hundred and fifty paces off, announces that he will shoot the side-blade and both sides must then go home, and hits it. Everyone goes home.

At Wan, Zhang Xiu surrenders and then revolts in the night over Cao Cao's treatment of his uncle's widow. Cao Cao escapes on a borrowed horse; his eldest son and his nephew are killed; and Dian Wei holds the gate on foot with no armour and both arms broken until he dies standing up, and no one dares pass him even then.
Cao Cao's public mourning is for Dian Wei, not for his son.
chapters.history: The archery feat is recorded in the histories, which is more than can be said for most of the novel's famous shots. The disaster at Wan is historical in every particular, including Dian Wei's death at the gate.

pins.note: Shoots the halberd at a hundred and fifty paces.
Saved by the shot.
Sent to destroy Liu Bei; goes home instead.
Loses his son, his nephew and his bodyguard in one night.
Dies on his feet in the gateway.
Surrenders, then revolts.
Now advising Zhang Xiu.

chapters.title: Yuan Shu Takes the Imperial Title; Cao Cao Borrows a Head
summary: Yuan Shu declares himself emperor on the strength of a stolen seal and a folk rhyme, and everyone who might have supported him stops. A coalition forms almost instantly.

Marching against him with a shortage of grain, Cao Cao tells his quartermaster to issue short measures, waits for the army to start muttering, then has the man beheaded for embezzlement and posts his head with a notice. The army is satisfied. It is the coldest thing in the book, and he does it in the middle of a chapter about someone else's treason.
chapters.history: Yuan Shu's usurpation destroyed him, as the novel says. The borrowed head is recorded in a commentary to the histories and the novel reproduces it almost unchanged.

pins.note: Declares himself emperor, and is abandoned.
Borrows his quartermaster's head.
Joins the coalition against Yuan Shu.
Breaks with Yuan Shu over the title.

chapters.title: Jia Xu Foresees a Victory; Xiahou Dun Eats His Own Eye
summary: Jia Xu, advising Zhang Xiu, tells him to pursue a retreating Cao Cao, and when that fails tells him to pursue again immediately — and is right both times, for reasons he explains afterwards with some patience.

Cao Cao turns on Lü Bu. At the siege lines Xiahou Dun takes an arrow through the left eye, pulls it out with the eyeball still on it, says 'the essence of my father and mother — I cannot throw it away', swallows it, and rides down the man who shot him.
chapters.history: Xiahou Dun really did lose an eye to an arrow and was called 'blind Xiahou' for it, to his lasting annoyance. Eating it is the novel's contribution.

pins.note: Right twice in a row, for reasons nobody else can see.
Turns on Lü Bu at last.
Loses an eye and swallows it.
Besieged.
Joins the siege.

chapters.title: Cao Cao Floods Xiapi; Lü Bu Dies at the White Gate Tower
summary: Cao Cao dams the Yi and the Si and lets them into the city. Lü Bu, who has stopped drinking and started forbidding it, alienates the last officers he has; they tie him up while he sleeps and open the gate.

At the White Gate Tower he offers to serve — 'you take the infantry, I will take the cavalry, and the empire is yours' — and Cao Cao wavers. He asks Liu Bei's opinion. Liu Bei says four words: 'Remember Ding Yuan and Dong Zhuo.' Lü Bu is strangled.
Chen Gong, offered his life, walks to the executioner without stopping. Zhang Liao curses everyone present and is untied by Cao Cao personally.
chapters.history: Historical, including Liu Bei's intervention — the one moment in the novel where his mildness drops entirely and he simply has a man killed.

pins.note: Strangled at the White Gate Tower.
Refuses his life.
Leaves the novel here without a word.
Curses his captors, and is spared.
'Remember Ding Yuan and Dong Zhuo.'

chapters.title: Cao Cao Hunts at Xutian; Dong Cheng Receives the Girdle Edict
summary: At the imperial hunt Cao Cao rides level with the Emperor, takes the Emperor's own bow to shoot the deer, and then keeps the bow. When the officers cheer the kill, he moves in front of the Emperor to receive it. Guan Yu reaches for his blade and Liu Bei stops him with a look.

That night the Emperor bites his finger and writes an edict in blood, sews it into a jade girdle, and gives the girdle to his father-in-law Dong Cheng as a gift, in public, with Cao Cao watching. Seven men eventually sign it. One of them is Liu Bei, who immediately starts growing vegetables to look harmless.
chapters.history: The girdle edict and Dong Cheng's conspiracy are historical, and so is its failure. The hunt at Xutian is the novel's staging of what the conspiracy was about.

pins.note: Takes the Emperor's bow, and keeps it.
Writes the edict in his own blood.
Receives the girdle.
Signs, then grows vegetables.
Reaches for his blade at the hunt.
Signs the edict and rides home.
Has finished Gongsun Zan and turns south.
